utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Madam Registrar, please proceed with calling the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, madam. Mr. Brdjanin, can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to all. Yes, I can follow in a language I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good morning to you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Ann Sutherland, Julian Nicholls, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to the three of you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman with Aleksandar Vujic and Kelli Sarrett.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Good morning to you and your colleagues. So, any preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have two matters that come under the heading "loose ends." We need to go into private session to talk about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go into private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't foresee that that witness will ever come for cross-examination, so it's not likely. It's a foregone conclusion, actually. When will Ms. Korner be back with us?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Monday, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Tomorrow's witness is in whose hands? Is it in your hands, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That will be Mr. Tieger, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought so. He lost his way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Treanor. I'll ask you to repeat -- could you kindly repeat your solemn declaration once more, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Good morning. You may sit down, and Mr. Ackerman will proceed with his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do we need both microphones switched on or is one sufficient?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How are you this morning?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very good, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I got yelled at by the translators after yesterday's session for going way too fast through difficult material, and I want to apologise first of all to the translators for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And see if you and I can help each other go a bit slower to give them a chance to do the fine job that they always do. Okay?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll do everything I can, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you catch me going too fast you let me know. So let's try to be a little more considerate of their job today. We left off yesterday with just kind of a reminder of January 11th, 1992, and the decision made by the Badinter Commission on that date. That's the event that prompted the proposition that a referendum be held in Bosnia-Herzegovina regarding the issue of independence, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, if we go back to October, when there was a -- sort of the first blow-up in the parliament, where the Serb delegates walked out and there was a vote to make the application for independence, basically. That wasn't a permanent split, Serb delegates returned to the parliament at a later date and they were present for the debate that then occurred on the 25th of January of 1992, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a couple of things there. I don't think the vote on the 14th of October was directly, literally a vote to apply for recognition. As for the participation of the SDS deputies in the assembly, they did continue to participate but on a selective basis, and they did not return en masse to the assembly. How many were present for the debate on the 20 -- was it the 25th or the 26th of January, I'm not sure, but certainly they were represented there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, the session lasted for 17 hours, so it may very well have been parts of both days. At that session, Momcilo Krajisnik was serving as president of the assembly, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the matter for discussion at that point was whether or not to hold this referendum. There was a resolution to hold a referendum, and that's what was being debated. And the Serb delegates, first of all, tried again to have the matter referred to the council for national equality that we talked about yesterday, which effort failed; yes?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then, when that failed, Mr. Krajisnik announced that the session was adjourned, and I think at that point the Serb delegates departed, Krajisnik was replaced by a member of the SDA, and the proposal to hold a referendum then was passed?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will have to take your word for that. I'm not familiar with the transcript of that session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't read the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My information about it is coming from Exhibit DB1, page 105. If we could take a look at it. It's right under the heading called "The parliamentary showdown." "The debate in parliament over the adoption of the referendum took place January 25 and ended when the Serb deputies withdrew after a majority consisting of Bosnian Muslim and Croat delegates turned down a Serb motion that the matter be placed before the not-yet-established council for national equality. When Momcilo Krajisnik, the Serb president of the assembly, attempted to adjourn the session, he was replaced by a member of the SDA and the proposal to hold a referendum was adopted in the absence of the SDS members in the form proposed by the Muslim deputies. The decision placed the Bosnian government and the Serbs on a collision course." Do you have any reason to dispute the contents of that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I say, I have not read the transcript of that session, so I cannot confirm or dispute the accuracy of what's written here. From the task that the Court set me yesterday to look into some of the statistics that were presented in this book, I have become a bit wary of what may be in this book in general. So I would not want to make a statement about the accuracy of any statement in this book without being familiar with the documentary basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly do accept the proposition that a resolution to hold the referendum was passed on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's stop here for a minute and go back to the task that you were asked to look into yesterday, and I take it from what you've just said you've done that.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could you tell us what you found.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. I have consulted the reports of the electoral commission on the balloting that was held beginning on the 18th of November, 1990. The electoral commission wrote three reports. They're all published in the Official Gazette of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There's one report regarding the elections for the Chamber of Citizens, another report for the elections to the Chamber of Municipalities, and another report for the elections to the Presidency. The report regarding the elections to the Chamber of Citizens, which I believe was the issue in question yesterday --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The question was: What are the invalid votes all about?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, in relation to the balloting. The report on the elections for that chamber report the results for each of the seven constituencies separately. They give the total number of people registered to vote and the total number of people that voted. The report does not give any indication of invalid ballots. It does toward the end of the report give percentages for the voting in each of those constituencies separately but does not give a total. It would appear from that report that the two figures in question are simply the total number of people registered and the total number of people voting, that is, the category of non-voting people simply seems to include those that did not go to the polls. It makes no reference at all to invalid ballots. The report of the electoral commission on the balloting for the presidency, since it is a -- what is done on a republic-wide basis, contains figures on a republic-wide basis for the total number of voters registered and for the total number of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. people voting, and it also includes a report on the number of invalid ballots, invalid ballots, in that election. It reports the number of invalid ballots as 127.291, which is out of a total of 2.339.958 people voting. So that is an invalid -- a rate of invalid ballots of something in the order of 5 per cent. Now, the book by Arnautovic on the elections of 1990 which was mentioned yesterday in connection with this matter contains a section on the results of the election. In the section on the results of the balloting for the Chamber of Citizens, on page 108, Arnautovic quotes the figures for voting in that election. However, the figures he gives actually come from the report on the balloting for the presidency. The essential point is that he notes that about three quarters of the people - and gives the exact figure - voted and repeats the statistic that I just gave, the figure, of invalid ballots and he says that's about 5.5 per cent. Now, I have -- or one of my staff members has in fact added up the numbers for the individual constituencies. Those numbers are a little bit different from the numbers that were reported as regards to the balloting for the Presidency. I don't know why. The total comes out to 3.018.206 registered voters in that voting, of whom 2.338.727 voted. So that's a turnout rate of about three quarters, which is consistent with Mr.Arnautovic says and consistent with what is reported about the presidential balloting and consistent with the figures reproduced in the table in the exhibit you showed me yesterday, except that that table labels those votes as invalid, and in fact it appears that they were not invalid ballots. Those were simply the percentage of people that did not go to the polls at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to look at the Oslobodjenje article from November 20th, 1990 that is listed as the source for this information?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I looked at the report of the electoral commission, which is the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I knew you had done that. I just wondered if you also looked at the Oslobodjenje?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Let me just finish the task that the Court set me yesterday. Arnautovic, on page 207 of his book, reproduces the text of the law on the elections, and this is in connection with the compulsory voting issue. Article 5 of that law states that -- I'm sorry, and this law was published in the Official Gazette of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina on 31 July 1990. Article 5 of that law states that: "A citizen registered in the general electoral list cannot be deprived of the list to vote nor can he be hindered in voting. The freedom of voting and the secrecy of voting is guaranteed. No one may -- can on any basis summon a voter to responsibility because of voting, nor demand of him that he say for whom he voted or why he has not voted." So I would infer from that that in conforming with general Yugoslav practice that voting was not compulsory.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The information that you have given us certainly is very important. I thank you for taking your time to dig this up.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you want to make that document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would -- he is your witness, basically. He's not a Court-appointed expert. So if you want to tender it, I have got nothing against and I would rather think it should be needed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have here copies --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No objection on your part then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- of the three electoral commission reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If that could be given Exhibit number P2683.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know the number, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's the next Prosecution number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So we'll have as soon as it is available we'll have photocopies made and we'll receive it in evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go back to this assembly session of January 25th now. Now, as I suggested, this session lasted for 17 hours. Are you aware that the reason for -- a major reason for the length of that session had to do with negotiations that were going on throughout the session in an effort to try to come to some kind of an agreement between the parties on the regionalisation of Bosnia so that all could agree with the referendum to support the referendum?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, I'm not familiar with what went on at that session per se. I certainly do know that there were negotiations going on in various fora, including the international, that attempted to seek an agreement among the parties in the republic, on the basis of some sort of regionalisation or cantonisation, I think was the term they were using at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. In Exhibit DB-1 on page 106, there is a quotation from Oslobodjenje's article regarding this session, which speaks of what went on there. It's a bit long, and I'm really not interested in reading the entire thing. It's on the ELMO. We should go up to the top that begins "During the course of the session." I'd invite you just to very briefly read through it and then perhaps you'll agree with me that what was going on was a serious effort to try to solve the issue, and it actually seems to have come quite close with an agreement between Muhamed Cengic and Radovan Karadzic, which apparently then got vetoed by Alija Izetbegovic, according to this article, if this article is accurate. Have you managed to read through it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm almost finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Take your time.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think the only question I have is just to invited you to comment on that if you feel you'd like to. Otherwise we can go on to the next document.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, all I can say is I know that a -- the proposal to hold the referendum was adopted at that session. I can't comment on the accuracy of that report, since I'm not familiar --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- with the documentation that might lead me to make a more well-founded statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's look now at Exhibit P102. It's now the next day, January 26th. There's apparently a meeting of the Assembly of the Republic of the Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina, at which some conclusions are adopted. And the first of those refers to the previous day's action in the republic assembly. The decision to hold a referendum for the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina which would be a basis for transforming Bosnia and Herzegovina into an independent state was adopted in an irregular manner and without the presence of the Serbian deputies. As an act by the legal representatives of the Muslim and Croat peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina, it can be binding only on members of those two peoples. For the Serbian people of Bosnia and Herzegovina, this decision is invalid and directed against their existential interests. Now, what's happening there is the Serbian representatives are declaring their position regarding the invalidity of the previous day's actions of the republic assembly, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is certainly the expressed view of the Bosnian-Serb assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm interested in whether you know anything about what the next paragraph means. It reads: "The decisions forbidding further work of BH representatives in all federal organs and institutions and replacing the governor of the BH National Bank are also null and void." Do you have any idea what that's about?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the specific decisions being referred to, but I can only infer, and it would seem to be within the logic of what was happening that there came a time when the -- one or another of the organs of the Socialist Republic, and I don't know which one and I don't know when, decided that that republic would no longer participate - I think it actually might have been on the 14th of October. I think one of those decisions points in that direction - that representatives of the republic would no longer participate in the federal Yugoslav institutions. I'm pretty sure that is in the 14 October -- one of the 14 October documents, one of the resolutions that was adopted over the objections of the SDS delegates. Now, the decision to dismiss the governor of the National Bank, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You don't know if that was the Serb governor of the National Bank that was dismissed by the --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: - Alija Izetbegovic government? Let's look now at paragraph 2. "At the conference of the legitimate representatives of the three state-forming peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina will endeavour to achieve agreement on the already initiated democratic transformation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the direction of finding the best state solution for each people. If this solution were to be common to all three peoples, then the democratic participation of the citizens and nations of BH in a referendum at which the achieved agreement would be confirmed could be acceptable to the assembly of the Serbian people." It appears to me that what they're saying there is we're not giving up on trying to arrive at an agreed solution to this problem. We still believe that there is a way to cantonise and then become independent with everyone in agreement. Isn't that what that says?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it certainly indicates that, and in fact negotiations did continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. All right. The next document I want to refer to is P36. Now, I think this document, Your Honours, has been admitted under three different numbers, P36, P106, and P2070. I believe those are all the same document. But in any event, the document that I'm interested in is a document of 3 February 1992, and it is a conclusion of the assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. So we've now gone from 26 January to 3 February, just a few days later. And there's an apparent meeting of the assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, where conclusions are adopted regarding the referendum. Paragraph 1 provides that municipal assemblies in the Autonomous Region of Krajina should not organise any activities regarding the holding of the referendum on an autonomous, sovereign, and independent Bosnia and Herzegovina scheduled for 21 February and 1 March 1992. In paragraph 2, "The referendum on an autonomous, sovereign, and independent Bosnia and Herzegovina is unconstitutional and illegal because it was called by an unauthorised organ in contravention of the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina. (The decision taken by the rump assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina without representatives of the Serbian people is an act of terror by the fiendish anti-Serbian coalition of the SDA, Party of Democratic Action, and the HDZ, Croatian Democratic Union, against the constituent Serbian people.) As such, it should not be conducted in the municipalities of the Autonomous Region of Krajina." Basically, what the assembly seems to be saying in this document is that since the decision to hold the referendum was taken without the participation of the Serbs as a constituent nation, it's illegal and unconstitutional, and therefore the legitimate organs of government, the municipalities, should not involve themselves in organising the holding of an illegally ordered referendum; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to take your word for what paragraph 1 says, since it's largely illegible on the screen here, but I think that is the sum and substance of what's going on here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll let you put -- I'll put my copy on the ELMO so you can read it, because I ...

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. And I'm wondering, Your Honour, if the Prosecution might want to substitute a clean copy for the exhibit that's not readable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think there is a need for that, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But the official record of this Tribunal is going to have a document that nobody can read if we don't substitute one that's readable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, I can give you mine, actually. No problem. But if you have a spare copy --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the Presiding Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry about that. Anyway, if you have a spare copy, Ms. Sutherland, you can make it available and we'll substitute one document for the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The next document I want to refer you to is DB164, which is a large document. It's the Official Gazette of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, year 1, issue number 4. It's a document that's about 140 pages long. In fact, it's exactly 140 pages long. On page 48 of that document, you'll find the law on internal affairs, beginning on that page. The document contains a number of laws: The law on government, law on National Defence, Internal Affairs, National Bank, a financial audit, public revenues, establishment of radio, TV. Right now I'm interested in the law on Internal Affairs and I'd like you to look at Article 32, which you'll find on page 54. Now, the law on Internal Affairs is basically the law that sets out the law and procedures regarding, among other things, the activities of the police, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Article 32 says this: "A Municipal Assembly and its Executive Council may submit their proposals and opinions to the ministry's head office and make motions regarding issues pertinent to security on the territory of the municipality and to the work of their security services centre and public security station. The ministry's head office is obligated to consider the proposals, opinions, and motions of the Municipal Assembly and its Executive Council and to reply to them, stating its stances and measures taken." This section provides that if a municipality has proposals, opinions, and motions regarding the operation of the police, that they should submit those to the head office of the ministry, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it seems to say here, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And once that has been submitted, then the ministry has an obligation, it looks to me like a firm obligation, to consider the proposals, opinions, and motions, and reply, informing the municipality as to their position regarding these issues and the measures that they're taking to implement or not implement the suggestions from the municipality; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The next article I want to refer you to is Article 46, and that's on page 58. This article basically speaks of special powers granted the minister of the interior and certain of the minister's authorised officers in the event of certain emergency situations. Let's look at the exact language: "In the discharge of duties and responsibilities to protect the constitutional order, the lives and personal safety of people, to protect property from destruction, damage, and theft, to maintain law and order and the safety of road traffic, as well as, in the event of general danger caused by natural disasters, epidemics, and so forth, the Minister or his authorised representative or, in emergencies, other authorised officers as well, may issue special orders to citizens, enterprises, and other legal entities." Now, there's nothing in there that mentions a state of war as one of the emergencies that would justify the minister exercising these extraordinary powers, is there, although one might extrapolate that from Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. some of the language.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it certainly does not limit it to that situation. It's much broader, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It speaks specifically, however, the natural disasters, epidemics, and things of that nature. But in any event, it does authorise the minister and other authorised officers of the ministry to issue special orders to citizens, enterprises, and other legal entities in case of an emergency situation that's outlined therein, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So in the appropriate emergency, the minister or other authorised ministry officer could issue binding orders to an enterprise, to - I don't know - to do something to assist the emergency, I suppose, or to a citizen, along the same line, all designed for the protection of constitutional order, lives, safety, property, maintaining law and order, road traffic, things of that nature; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would only add that in my reading of the original of this article, there is no "et cetera." It seems to be limited to natural disasters and epidemics.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So after epidemics, the "et cetera" doesn't appear. That raises an interesting issue, and we might as well look at it now, because I don't know the answer to it. Keep that document and take a look at P2330. P2330, sir, is another copy, another translation, apparently, of the same law on Internal Affairs. And the language of Article 46 is slightly different, and it's been my assumption that that's a translation difference rather than a change in the law. But you're correct; it doesn't include the "et cetera" in this translation.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So it's just -- it's the same -- it's the same law, just translated slightly differently; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It appears to be, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. If -- in an appropriate emergency, then, it seems, and if - and this is a big "if" - if the ARK Crisis Staff were a legal entity, which I think it probably was not, but if the ARK Crisis Staff were a legal entity, in an emergency the minister of the interior could issue orders to the ARK Crisis Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although one would have thought that if this was meant -- "other legal entities" was meant to include sociopolitical organisations, such as the municipalities, it would have said that, and not merely lump them under the rubric of other legal entities. But that's a matter of legal drafting and whatnot that I'm not competent to comment on. I just point that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It may be a legal expert from the former Yugoslavia would be able to tell us that legal entities is a term of art that has specific meaning, and I don't know whether it is or not. But we may come to that some day. I want you to look now --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says legal persons in the original. In legal parlance, maybe legal entities, but, I don't know, to me, that wouldn't be a given in my mind that it would include sociopolitical organisations which is another well-recognised and established concept in Yugoslav law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're saying in the Serbo-Croatian, as you translate it, that should be translated legal persons rather than legal entities?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the way I would translate it. I'm not sure whether there is a difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't forget, Mr. Ackerman, that we're dealing with a country where you have a civil law basis, and in civil law countries, the notion of physical persons as against moral persons under the philosophy of law is somewhat different from how you learn it in the States or how I learnt it in my country or how you learn it ... So you've got body corporate, moral persons, those which are legally constituted, those which are not incorporated, and so it gets complicated. So it's not just a matter of translation. It's a matter of knowing exactly what falls under which category of persons, legal persons, under Bosnian law or under Yugoslav law. And frankly, if you ask me, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't have forgotten that, Your Honour, because I never knew it. I appreciate your pointing that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But do take that into consideration, because under civil law the notion of persona for the purposes of rights and obligations is somewhat more limited than it is under common law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I think we're finished with that, but I do want to -- just while we're talking about translations, ask you this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In the course of preparing your reports, and because you are apparently quite fluent in Serbo-Croat, did you find that a lot of the translations of documents that you were consulting were inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we don't use translations, in principle, and we work from the original documents. In cases where we easily know the translation ERN number, because it appears on an exhibit list or something like that, we will put it into the report as a -- in order to facilitate matters for the -- for readers that may not know the language. But we do not use the translations, per se. We do not check the translations. Obviously, we -- myself and people in my section have occasion to set eyes on translations, and we sometimes do find that we do not agree with those translations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you say "we," who are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Myself and my staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You understand that the Trial Chamber does rely on translations, since the Trial Chamber is -- does not have the fluency in Serbo-Croat like you do, and so even though you don't rely on translations, this Court does, and to a great extent, the judgement in this case will rely on those translations. And so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The question I -- okay. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor has already said that he doesn't rely on translations, so he's not in a position to answer Mr. Ackerman's question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't think she's heard the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is very relevant, of course. It is very relevant, because there is a suggestion being made by Mr. Ackerman that while -- that the translations that are made available to the Court may not always be that reliable. And he was trying to get the witness to deal with this subject, even though the witness has said that he himself and his staff do not rely on the translations but on the originals. But maybe he is in a position to tell us why he relies on the originals rather than on translations, whether it is because from his own experience he finds that translations are sometimes unreliable or whether -- I don't know. I mean, it's up to the witness himself to clarify this. But it's certainly a relevant question. So, Mr. Treanor, more or less I take it that you understand where Mr. Ackerman is heading. I don't think he needs to finish his question until -- unless Mr. Ackerman himself thinks that he ought to finish his question. Mr. Ackerman, can the witness answer your question or do you want to conclude it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think you're right. I think he probably knows where I'm going. If he does, he can answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I know where you're going, and I will comment on that issue to the best that I can. And if that doesn't sufficiently enlighten the Court, I'm prepared to answer any other question in that regard. I've been involved in doing research and analysis using foreign language sources for over 30 years, multiple languages from multiple archives and countries, this, that, and the other thing. I never had the luxury of having a translator translate them for me, so I took the trouble to learn the appropriate languages, to a sufficient degree that I was able to perform my research and analysis. That's just the way I work. That's the way the people in my section work. They had similar experiences. So we brought that experience to this institution and those methods to this institution. When we add to that the fact that in very many, if not virtually every case, after a document was acquired, there would be a lapse of sometimes considerable time in having a translation done, and indeed sometimes translations are never done. Sometimes they're only done once we call attention to a document. Anyways, we're in a position to immediately start using the given document in the original language in our further research and analysis. So the issue of translations is not one that easily occurs to us. It only comes to our attention when someone draws it to our attention or when very frequently by chance, as indeed in the course of my testimony here, that we have the opportunity to see a translation side by side with the original. I have in the course of my testimony, I believe spontaneously on a number of occasions, called the Court's attention to translations with which I disagreed. But again, this is only on a rather chance basis. It is not the job of my section, and I have -- I may say stoutly resisted any move in that direction to translate documents or to revise translations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand that completely. I did just kind of a quick count just now in my head. I think since we started yesterday, you and I, we've looked at about 20 documents, and in three or four of those documents you pointed out what you believed were translation errors, which would be an error rate of, I think, 15 or 20 per cent. I find that to be sort of frighteningly significant, don't you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would depend. It would depend on the error.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, the next question becomes whether --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: And indeed, let me also comment. There can be legitimate and there is legitimate disagreements among translators of equal qualifications of how they may translate things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's where I was just going --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The persons/entities -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The question becomes whether your translation is the correct one or whether the professional translators in CLSS have made the correct call, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. But if there is in fact an error rate of 15 or 20 per cent, that's a significant situation in a case where the question is whether or not matters have been proven beyond a reasonable doubt?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this is an inappropriate question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: These are submissions, but I'm letting him carry on because I want to see how weak or weaker his argument is. So let him finish. Mr. Ackerman is an experienced lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: He's making argument --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's also giving an indication of how strong his argument is, and that's why I let him go on, because then I am in a position to make an assessment on how strong the submission is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And he's understood. He's shifting to another area straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to go now to April 6th and some of the events subsequent to April 6th. April 6th was the day that the European Community granted recognition to Bosnia-Herzegovina; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so. Again, 5th, 6th, 7th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at DB165, please. DB165 is a document dated 15 April, about a week after independence had been granted, recognised. This is a decision of the Presidency, using the emergency powers of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, first of all declaring a state of imminent threat of war, and second of all, ordering mobilisation of the Territorial Defence in the whole territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then we see later, further down in that document, that the assembly then confirmed that decision on 12th of May of 1992.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you recall what date it was that Izetbegovic issued his declaration of imminent threat of war and mobilised the TO in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The precise date, no. I think it was shortly after the recognition date. I'm not positive, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And prior to the 15th of April, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I believe so, but I don't have the document in mind, so I ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, if we go, then, to document P153. P153, the next day after this declaration. Then the Defence Minister of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina issues some decisions and an explanation. It refers to the order of the Presidency. In paragraph 1, it says that: "The Territorial Defence of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina shall be established as an armed force of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Command and control will be exercised." And it says something about the municipal district and regional staffs, the republican staff of the SBih TO. In the second decision, a state of imminent threat of war is declared, general public mobilisation of the TO in the entire territory of the Serbian Republic of BiH is hereby ordered. All military conscripts have to make themselves available to TO staffs. Finally, down in the explanation right at the very end, "In the preparations for training and deployment of the TO units, effect cooperation with the JNA units and, where possible, establish unified command." So the next day, April 16th, the minister is issuing his orders regarding this matter.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, the next document I want you to look at is -- and keep that document. Look at P167 now, please. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Now, the document we've just been looking at from Subotic is decision number 1/92 of 16 April 1992, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one we just looked at previous to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, the Subotic decision.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look now at this document, P167, in the preamble you'll see it's issued pursuant to the Subotic decision that we just looked at.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, the Subotic decision was 16 April. The decision we're looking at now, by Milorad Sajic, doesn't happen for about 18 days. It happens about 18 days later, on 4 May of 1992, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, to the extent that it orders a mobilisation, calls for a mobilisation, I take it it's a bit redundant, since Subotic did that two weeks before, unless, of course, no one paid any attention to Subotic.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the face of it it would seem to be redundant. Again I don't know what the legal niceties are.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But presumably if Subotic ordered it two and a half weeks before, there should have been no need for Sajic to order it two and a half weeks later. But in any event, that's what the document says. Plus it does have some additional language regarding curfew and surrender of weapons by paramilitary formations and individuals, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. If one wants to view this document, and I suppose one could view this document as an implementation within the Autonomous Region of Krajina of Subotic's order, simply passing it along, then one wonders why it took that many days for it to happen. Do you have any idea?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look now -- let's -- well, just a minute. Let's look now at P188. And I hope you've still got the Subotic order, because --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. That's P153. I'm sorry. We need P153 back, along with P188. Now, P153, back there in April, ordered a mobilisation of the TO in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Then we come to this decision on 12 May, a bit less than a month -- about three weeks later. And Article 2 of this decision -- first of all, Article 1 says that the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina is hereby formed. Article 2 then takes those TO units that were mobilised by Subotic and says with regard to them: "Former Territorial Defence units and staffs are hereby renamed as units and commands of the army, the organisation and formations of which shall be determined by the president of the Republic." So those TO units are just being taken basically out of the All People's Defence category and brought into the army as units of the regular VRS at this point, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I might state it as -- in the following manner, that the Territorial Defence is being sort of converted into the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: As I understand it, they actually became light brigades or something like that in the army.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my understanding as well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The other thing that you see kind of fairly clearly in this Article 2 is that the president of the Republic is in effect the commander-in-chief of the army.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I think, Your Honour, this would be an appropriate point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, we are going to have a short break, 25 minutes, which means 25 minutes from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The next document I want to look at, sir, is P222. This is a decision, presumably of Dr. Radovan Karadzic of 31 May, 1992. It provides in Article 1, "War Presidencies shall be formed in municipalities of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina where the assembly and executive organs are unable to exercise their authority." So it follows that the pattern in Article 1, that we've seen before, that emergency bodies can be implemented where the assembly is unable to meet, exercise its authority, and in this case also including the executive organs; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It then talks in Article 3 about what that War Presidency should do. "It should organise, coordinate, and adjust activities for the defence of the Serbian people and for the establishment of the lawful municipal authorities. It should perform all duties of the assembly and the executive organ until those organs are able to convene and work. It should create and ensure conditions for the work of military organs and units in defending the Serbian people, and carry out other tasks of state organs if they are unable to convene." Correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then finally in Article 5, it says that these War Presidencies had to be formed within 15 days of the date of this decision, or by basically the middle of June and on that date the Crisis Staffs would cease to operate; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Article 2 sets out the composition. The War Presidency consists of a republic commissioner, and then generally the president of the Municipal Assembly or his deputy, or the vice-president, president of the Executive Committee or his deputy, or the vice-president; or a citizen chosen from among the representatives or committee members. Are you aware of any War Presidency that was formed anywhere in Bosnia-Herzegovina, headed by a republic commissioner, appointed by the president, with the membership set out in Article 2?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, let me just say that this is a decision signed by Radovan Karadzic, but it states in the preamble it was taken by the presidency rather than by him personally. I have seen numerous appointments of war commissioners. I have not seen - which doesn't mean they don't exist or we don't have them - documents which would set out the - I'm sure we do have them, but I can't recall them to mind. I think I just was looking at one. No. It's of an earlier date. Sorry - setting out the exact composition of the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Tell us this: Tell us which municipality in the Autonomous Region of Krajina that we are concerned with did away with its Crisis Staff and established a War Presidency that was headed by a republic commissioner appointed by the president, by the presidency.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware that any -- I've not seen a document appointing any war commissioner in the ARK region.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. So as far as you know, this decision was ignored by every municipality in the Autonomous Region of Krajina. You couldn't show us otherwise, could you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can only state in that regard, and this issue is extremely confused, and the documentation on it is incomplete, that there was a decision which I think was referred to in my direct examination issued by the same body, that is, the presidency, about ten days later, which, on the face of it, explicitly stated that it abolished this decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Trust me, we're going there. But I would like you to answer the question I did ask you. So far as you know, this decision was ignored by every municipality in the Autonomous Region of Krajina. You couldn't show us otherwise, could you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, the word "ignored," I don't know what happened precisely. Obviously, this decision was deemed to be problematic by the presidency, and they changed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, let me try it a different way. Can you tell me one municipality in the Autonomous Region of Krajina that implemented this decision in its terms?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the precise terms set out here, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Let's go, then, to Exhibit P269, which is the next document and the one you were talking about. Now, this is the one that you were alluding to in your answer to my previous questions. This one is dated 10 June 1992, again presumably signed by Dr. Radovan Karadzic. And it's a very similar document, again a decision, and this time it calls for formation of War Commissions in the war-afflicted municipalities of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or where there is a threat of war; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And again, it sets out the composition of these War Commissions. A War Commission shall consist of a republic commissioner. And if you look at Article 4, that republic commissioner is to be appointed by the presidency. So the War Commission shall consist of republic commissioner and four members chosen from among the most prominent citizens on crisis staffs, the business community and the ruling party. In other words, a five-member War Commission; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It says in Article 5 that this should happen within 15 days, or otherwise by the 25th of June. It says that crisis staffs cease to operate once the War Commissions are established. And it annuls the prior decision that we were talking about?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: To create War Presidencies; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, neither of these decisions says anything about regional organisations, regional crisis staffs, anything of that nature, does it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Again, let me ask you this: Do you know of any municipality in the Autonomous Region of Krajina which, in response to this decision, formed a War Commission consisting of five members, headed by a republic commissioner appointed by the presidency?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, I'll have to rephrase that. In the terms of this document, it wasn't for the municipality to form the War Commissions; it was for the presidency to appoint a war commissioner. The war commissioner would form the commission. And as I stated previously, I have not seen, although I have seen numerous appointments of war commissioner, I have not seen the appointment of a war commissioner to an ARK municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. If you look again basically at both of these documents, what is clear from these documents in terms of a line of authority is that it's clearly a line of authority from the presidency to the municipalities, with no intervening regional body of any kind involved; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no mention in either of these documents of regional organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's look now at P270, please. Now, both of those prior documents that we were just looking at were called decisions. The one you're looking at now, P270 document, is called a decree. Do you have any idea what the difference is between a decision and a decree?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this a translation question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't know whether it is or not. Is it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd need to see the original of the document. I'm sorry. Can I see the translation? Yes, I would translate that as "decision."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. So you would say that decree --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it was translated -- the same word was translated in that manner in the previous documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. This one is dated 13 June 1992. "The formation or activity of any self-organised armed groups and individuals is hereby prohibited on the territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Existing groups and individuals shall be obliged to place themselves under the sole command of either the army or of the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina within three days." Article 3, submission to the sole command of the army or the police also implies strict observance for the strictures of international law. This is a decision of 13 June 1992. Can you tell us if this decision was implemented in the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That gets a little bit beyond the sphere of my competence. I would say, and I'm trying to --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll accept --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were efforts to implement it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm perfectly willing to accept that it's not within your competence, if that's the position you want to take. That's okay with me. I won't insist on an answer. But if you do have an answer, I'd appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Finally, I want to look again, because I think you may not agree with me about this. I want to look again at P285. We looked at it yesterday. And just to draw your attention to it again. And maybe you don't even need to look at it. This is the assembly session of the Autonomous Region of Krajina in which they considered and approved the decisions of the ARK Crisis Staff and War Presidency, or whatever it was called. You recall that, on 17 July 1992?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the document we saw yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And once the assembly met on July 17th and considered the decisions of the Crisis Staff -- by the way, we don't have any idea what decisions and conclusions were considered, since there's no list of them, do we?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But in any event, once this happened, that signified the end of the ARK Crisis Staff, didn't it? It didn't function after that; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think -- I think there are indications that it did, which are discussed in the addendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I know you discussed that in the addendum, but I couldn't Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. find, and I looked pretty hard - I couldn't find any decision or conclusion of the Crisis Staff after that date. Look at P273, for instance. Now, as far as I know, P273, dated the second day of July, 1992, is the last document to come out of the ARK Crisis Staff. And this is a document that's actually issued and signed by Boro Blagojevic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it appears to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it appears that in this document, Boro Blagojevic, on behalf of the Crisis Staff, is appointing some kind of a coordinating body that Mr. Brdjanin is part of, plus some other people. My question is: Do you know of any conclusion or decision or document issued by the ARK Crisis Staff after 2 July 1992?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not offhand. I think there's a table in the -- one of the appendices to the addendum that lists all the decisions that we have been able to recover.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it's certainly the last one that I think is in any of the documents that we have existing. The only other thing I would point out is, as late as 2 July 1992, this staff, according to this document, continues to call itself a Crisis Staff, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We certainly have reference in the letterhead here to the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Treanor, I want you to know that I appreciate your efforts to answer my questions and to give as full and complete answers as you could. I really do appreciate that. And I don't have any more questions for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Ms. Sutherland, is there going to be a re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Mr. Ackerman intimated that he would take approximately an hour, so I may have to take an early break at some stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's up to you. Do you prefer to take a break now?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. Just a short break to get the documents together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much time do you require?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Is that okay with you, Mr. Ackerman? Mr. Treanor, we have to have another short break. I'm sure you understand why. And we will reconvene in ten minutes' time, all right? And after that -- how long do you think your re-examination will take, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, you know I'm a bad estimator of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you say one hour usually it means one day, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm hesitant to say, but not more than an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic used to tell me that: I'm hesitant to say. We need to plan, because we're taking a ten-minute break now and we will require another 25-minute break later. We need to know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just -- I don't think you heard me. I said I don't think I will be not more than an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So we'll have a ten-minute break now and then we see what the position, what the situation is afterwards. Thank you. --- Break taken at 11.22 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please be seated. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could Mr. Treanor be given Exhibit P2351, please. It's his addendum report. Mr. Treanor, yesterday Mr. Ackerman took you to page 5 of your report, paragraph E6, and questioned you in relation to the variant A/B document of 19th December 1991. That paragraph, E6, that's contained in the executive summary, is it not?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you expanded more in your report with respect to this document on pages 22 and following; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could check the page number. In regard to this issue in general, I followed up on this myself. That particular document in the issue of the establishment of the crisis staffs is dealt with in paragraphs 37 through 45 of the current exhibit, as well as in paragraphs 60 through 64 of Exhibit 2352, which is what I call the main report.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. And in fact, paragraph 37 starts -- is on page 22 of the report. Mr. Ackerman questioned you about any evidence that anybody created a Crisis Staff because of this document. I want to take you now to several documents, and we can hopefully spend a brief time in relation to that. Can you look at this first document, and may it be marked as Exhibit P2684. Mr. Treanor, that's conclusions of the SDS --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me. Are we going to be favoured with a copy of this? Wait until --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- Mr. Ackerman. Do you have a copy now, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And this is the document that was disclosed to the Defence --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Today, at this moment, Your Honour. It's dealing with a municipality which is not within the ARK region. But, as we will see, it's in relation to the variant A/B document and the issue that Mr. Ackerman raised yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, this is a document, the conclusions of the SDS Zvornik municipal board meeting held on the 22nd of December, 1991, some three days after the instructions dated the 19th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We can see in that document that the Crisis Staff is elected, in paragraph 3?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman also asked you questions yesterday about whether there was any documents where the person in charge of the Crisis Staff was referred to as a commander.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And we can see here that Branko Grujic is listed as the commander of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman also asked you questions yesterday about whether -- and this was in relation to the set-up of the Crisis Staff, whether there was a coordinator for negotiations with the other two parties, namely, the SDA and the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we go to paragraph 4, we can see that Jovo Ivanovic is elected coordinator for negotiations with the SDA and that he will appoint a negotiating team.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So while there's no explicit reference to the instructions in this document, is it your view that these conclusions reached at the meeting were based on those instructions?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My conclusion would certainly be that given the date of the documents and the language of the document, that these conclusions are based on the 19 December instructions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. I've finished with that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can we have Exhibit P865.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, this exhibit is the minutes of the 6th meeting of the executive committee of the SDS municipal board in Kljuc held on the 23rd of December, 1991. If I can draw your attention to agenda item 1. Does that show that decisions were made pursuant to the December 19 instructions?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item number 1 in the agenda?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. Veljko Kondic and following.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: AD-1. Okay. Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And he informs the meeting of the instructions for the organisation and activities of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: All organs will be required to act in accordance with the instructions.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Looking now at --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit P2063. In order to save time, perhaps the usher can take this document from me and place it on the ELMO machine. This is an extract from the minutes of the third session of the Executive Committee of the Bosanska Krupa Serbian Municipal Assembly held on the 24th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, looking at those minutes, can it be seen whether they were relying on the 19 December 1991 instructions? I think if I can take you to AD-3(A).

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the agenda at that point there is reference to implementing the instructions on establishing a Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit P1153.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, you know how heavily document-based this case is, and I think if Ms. Gustin has a list of --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: She's provided it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. So you have it now. All right. Okay. Yes. Okay. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, these -- Exhibit P1153 are the abridged minutes of the meeting of the Prijedor SDS and the SDS assemblymen's club on the 27th of December, 1991. If I can take you to paragraph 1, does this document show reliance on the December 1991 instructions? I'm sorry. Under proceedings.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under proceedings there is a reference to --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This clearly cannot be, because it says it's from the assembly, and the A/B document was not from the assembly. So I just point out that the conclusion he's being asked to draw would be incorrect if he did it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But let him comment on it, because the witness can read as much as you can, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, my response was going to be: There is reference to the instructions forwarded to the Prijedor SDS municipal board by the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I could not say with certainty, based on that wording, that this is what's being referred to, that is the 19 December document is being referred to. In order to strengthen any supposition that it is, I would have to see the original to make sure that the original word in the title of the document was being used, but the reference to the assembly is certainly problematic in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the same applies to the paragraph numbered 1, further up, before the section "proceedings," and that's the agenda items, okay? And that's the implementation of the decisions and positions taken again by the assembly of the Serbian people of BH. So we are still in the same waters there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and there had been a session of the assembly on the 21st of December.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, if I can take you to the second paragraph under paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Under proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The subparagraph 2 of paragraph 1, under "proceedings." Since there were two versions, only version 2, which is relevant to Prijedor municipality, was read out. Further, having read out all of the items in sections A and B of version 2, Miskovic explained what had to be done so far with respect to the instructions. Given that the 19 December 1991 instructions had two stages, would the reference there to sections A and B in version 2 make it likely that they were referring in fact to the December 19 instructions?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this certainly strengthens any conclusion that that document is what is being discussed. I am not familiar with any assembly document among those adopted on the 21st of December that would fit that description. Again, one of my first steps in this regard would be to check the original wording used for instructions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: B/C/S is available for you if you want to review it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suggest it's put on the ELMO so that the accused himself can at least follow, and Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't have page 1 here. In the line right below Arabic numeral 1, I do see the word "uputstvo," instructions, translated as instructions in the translation we saw used, and that is the word that is used in the title of the 19 December document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. I've finished with that document. Could you now be shown --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is also used further on in the document at the other passage that was referred to, which is several lines below that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you also see the use of the word "assembly"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, by the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could the witness be shown this document. Could it be marked as P2685. Again, Your Honour, this is a new document, because it's concerning a municipality which is not within the ARK region.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, this is notes of a Crisis Staff meeting of the SDS for the city of Sarajevo. Looking at this document, is the reference to the variant A/B document? And may I say: This document is dated Sarajevo 24 December 1991.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see any -- may I take this off? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: After listing the members of the Crisis Staff, 1 to 9 --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says: "Particular tasks as per the instructions on the organisation and activity of organs of the Serbian people in BH in emergency situations, according to Variant B, under first-degree instructions."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ackerman, do you accept that this document forms part -- be admitted, in other words, or not? Do you contest its authenticity?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've always contested the authenticity of documents that don't have signatures and stamps, and so I would do the same with regard to this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. It's still being admitted under the usual caveat.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit P1819.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This exhibit are the minutes from the first meeting of the party secretariat from the municipality of Bosanski Petrovac, dated the 26th of December, 1991. In that document, is there explicit reference to the instructions?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps you could point me to the paragraph you're interested in.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I can take you to item 2.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 2. Yes, that appears to be a reference to the same documents. It refers to it by its title.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And in fact, it says that the document needs to be typed in seven copies and every member of the secretariat is to be given a copy?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I've finished with that document. If the witness could be shown a new document, and could it be marked Exhibit P2686. Again, Your Honour, this is just being disclosed because it deals with the municipality that falls outside the Autonomous Region Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This exhibit are minutes from a session of the municipal board of the Trnovo SDS held on the 27th of December, 1992. If I can take you to the last paragraph, the subparagraph, under paragraph 2. I'm sorry. The top of page 2, after the persons named.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think we have it.
